description: Run a script on Linux instance to perform memory acquisition

limePath.description: (Optional) Path to the LiME Kernel module on disk. If not provided, LiME will be downloaded and built

AccessKeyId.description: (Required) AccesskeyID to store evidence details in S3.

SecretAccessKey.description: (Required) SecretAccessKey to store evidence details in S3

SessionToken.description: (Required) SessionToken to store evidence details in S3.

memoryAcquisitionTools.description: (Optional) Comma separated acquisition tools to try, in order. Each is attempted until one produces a capture containing a kernel banner. Supported values: lime, avml.

runCommand: # Linux memory acquisition. This runs on the instance under investigation.
# Two independent tools, tried in the order given by memoryAcquisitionTools,
# with the kernel banner check deciding whether a capture is usable and
# therefore whether to move on to the next tool.
# The fallback exists because LiME intermittently returns a full size image
# whose pages are almost entirely zero and which contains no kernel banner:
# 3 of 9 acquisitions observed here, across Amazon Linux 2 kernel 4.14 and
# Amazon Linux 2023 kernels 6.1 and 6.18. The cause is not isolated. What
# makes a second tool worth having rather than simply retrying the first is
# that the two fail for unrelated reasons: LiME is a kernel module mapping
# physical ranges, while AVML reads /dev/crash, /dev/mem or /proc/kcore. Two
# independent mechanisms with the same failure rate still multiply.
# Both write LiME format - verified from the header magic 454d 694c on an AVML
# capture - so the investigation side needs no knowledge of which tool ran,
# and Volatility 3 uses the same layer either way. Which tool did run is
# recorded in the capture's S3 metadata, because for evidence that is not
# Tool pins. Both are verified before use: LiME by cloning a tag, AVML by
# digest. Note the LiME repository moved - 504ensicsLabs/LiME now redirects to
# jtsylve/LiME, its original author - and cloning the old path works only
# while GitHub honours that redirect, which would silently resolve elsewhere
# if the old name were ever reclaimed. v1.12.0 is master minus one commit, and
# that commit only fixes license detection.
# One digest per release asset, because the release ships a build per
# architecture and downloading the wrong one produces a binary that cannot
# execute. A Graviton target used to get the x86_64 asset, so AVML was
# unavailable on exactly the architecture where it is the only option - LiME
# needs a kernel module and there is no aarch64 module to stage, only an in-guest
# compile. Digests taken from two independent downloads of v0.20.0.
# Named, not guessed. The release has no build for this machine type, so the
# attempt loop will report avml unavailable and move on to LiME.
# Why AWS credentials arrive as document parameters rather than an instance role:
# these are short-lived STS session credentials, minted per acquisition by the
# forensic Lambda with a session policy scoped to this case's S3 prefix - not
# long-lived IAM access keys. The host this runs on cannot be given an instance
# profile for the evidence bucket: it is either the machine under investigation,
# whose configuration must not be changed mid-incident, or an analysis host that
# must not hold standing access to other cases' evidence. Do not copy this
# pattern into a workload where an IAM role is available.
cd "$W" || fail 'cannot create the tool directory'
# $1 = artefact suffix, everything after it is passed to the aws cli as is.
# gcc and make are not present on the Amazon Linux 2023 AMI, and the
# LiME Makefile needs both plus the matching kernel headers.
sudo yum install git gcc make -y || { echo 'unable to install the LiME build tools' >&2; return 1; }
# Amazon Linux 2023 names kernel sub-packages per kernel line
# (kernel6.18-devel) from the 6.12 line onwards, while the 6.1 line and
# Amazon Linux 2 keep the unversioned kernel-devel name.
sudo yum install "kernel${kernel_line}-devel-$1" -y || sudo yum install "kernel-devel-$1" -y || { echo "no kernel-devel package for $1" >&2; return 1; }
sudo apt-get -y install git || { echo 'unable to install git' >&2; return 1; }
sudo apt-get install -y "linux-headers-$1" || { echo "no linux-headers package for $1" >&2; return 1; }
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential || { echo 'unable to install build-essential' >&2; return 1; }
echo "no kernel build tree for $1 - cannot compile LiME" >&2
# Pinned. An unpinned clone builds whatever the default branch is on the
# day of the incident, into a module loaded into the kernel of the machine
git clone --depth 1 --branch "$LIME_REF" "$LIME_REPO" LiME || { echo "LiME clone of $LIME_REF failed" >&2; return 1; }
make || { echo 'LiME module build failed' >&2; return 1; }
test -s "$LIME_MODULE" || { echo "the LiME build produced no lime-$1.ko" >&2; return 1; }
# Check for the module that was asked for, not for any file in the
# directory: `ls -A` was true for a failed download that left a partial or
# 4444 decimal is 115C hex and state 0A is TCP_LISTEN. /proc/net/tcp is the
# kernel's own socket table, so it sees LiME's kernel socket even on hosts
# where neither iproute2 nor net-tools is installed. 0100007F is 127.0.0.1
# in its byte order; matching the port alone also accepted a wildcard
# listener owned by an unrelated process as proof that LiME was ready.
# Wait for the module to be in the kernel AND for something to be
# listening. The original slept 120 seconds and then piped from the port
# regardless: with insmod failed that uploaded a ~20 byte gzip of empty
# input plus a sha256 of nothing, and exited 0.
echo "the LiME module for $kernel_release did not load or is not listening" >&2
# Tests the property directly rather than trusting the mount options: a
# trivial script written into the directory, made executable, and run.
if ! chmod +x "$probe" 2>/dev/null ; then rm -f "$probe"; return 1; fi
# Staged by the operator, who owns its provenance - the same contract
# the RHEL document uses, and what lets a host with no route to GitHub
echo "AVML publishes no build for $(uname -m) - nothing to download" >&2
[ -s "$W/avml" ] || { echo 'the downloaded AVML binary is empty' >&2; return 1; }
echo "AVML ${AVML_VERSION} ${AVML_ASSET} failed digest verification - expected $AVML_SHA256, got $actual" >&2
# /tmp is mounted noexec on a CIS hardened host, and chmod cannot undo that,
# so the binary is relocated to the first directory where an executable
# actually runs. Without this AVML is silently unavailable on exactly the
# hardened hosts most likely to be worth imaging. LiME is unaffected: insmod
# does not need the module to be executable.
echo "relocated AVML to $exec_dir because $W is mounted noexec" >&2
echo "no directory permits execution - cannot run AVML on this host" >&2
# AVML connects outward, so this side has to listen - the opposite of LiME,
# which listens and is connected to. The listener installs nothing on a host
# that may be compromised, and the capture still never touches its disk.
# The interpreter is resolved rather than assumed, and the script is
# deliberately valid under both Python 3 and Python 2. The stock Amazon Linux
# 2 EC2 AMI does ship python3 - measured on a live 4.14.355 instance, which
# has both python3 and python2.7 - but the amazonlinux:2 container image ships
# only python2.7, so a host built from a minimal base or with python3 removed
# would silently lose the fallback. AL2 kernel 4.14 is one of the kernels on
# which LiME produced an unusable capture, so it is the last place to accept
# an assumption in exchange for nothing.
for candidate in python3 python2 python; do
echo 'no python interpreter on this host - AVML has nothing to stream to' >&2
# Ask the binary what it is, rather than recording what the pin says it
# should be. For a staged binary those are different claims: the operator may
# have staged any build, and writing the pinned version into the evidence
# metadata would attribute the capture to a version that never ran. This also
# turns a binary that cannot execute at all - a text file staged by mistake,
# the wrong architecture - into an immediate, named failure instead of a
# 180 second wait for a connection that never comes.
echo "the AVML binary at $AVML_BIN ($AVML_ORIGIN) does not run - cannot acquire with it" >&2
# The pin was verified by digest, so a disagreement here means the
# release itself changed its self-reported version. Say so; do not stop.
# Bounded so a tool that never connects cannot hang the whole step.
# The listener binds immediately; AVML is delayed so it cannot connect
# before there is anything to connect to.
# exec, so the subshell is replaced by AVML and $! is AVML's own pid rather
# than the subshell's. That matters because of what has to happen next.
# AVML is reaped here, in the function that started it, and not in
# avml_cleanup: this function runs as an element of a pipeline, which bash
# executes in a subshell, so a pid recorded here is invisible to the parent
# and a kill there would silently never fire. The listener only returns once
# AVML closed the connection or the timeout expired, so by this point AVML has
# either finished - making the kill a no-op - or is stuck and must not be left
# running: a surviving AVML dials 4444 during a later attempt, which is the
# port LiME listens on, and would consume that capture out from under the
# Only the error file, which is on disk and so does cross the subshell
# boundary that the pid could not.
# Echoes a reason and returns 1 when the capture is not usable.
# $1 is the attempt number this call is judging. It matters because the key
# is the same on every attempt: if a second attempt's upload fails after tee
# has already finished - so the pipeline still succeeds - head-object returns
# the *first* attempt's object, which would then be accepted and reported as
# the second tool's capture, with the first tool's digest and metadata. The
# object's own acquisition-attempt says which attempt wrote it.
echo "the stored capture was written by attempt ${stored_attempt:-unknown}, not attempt $for_attempt - this attempt did not upload"
# The probe is written by a process substitution, which bash does not wait
# for, so give it a bounded moment to land.
for i in $(seq 1 60); do [ -s "$banner_probe" ] && break; sleep 1; done
# Inconclusive, not negative. Never discard a possibly good capture on a
# timing artefact, and never fall back on one either - the investigation
# checks the capture again before analysing it.
echo "BANNER CHECK INCONCLUSIVE for ${uploaded_bytes} compressed bytes" >&2
echo "no kernel banner in ${uploaded_bytes} compressed bytes of ${S3_EXPECTED_SIZE} bytes of RAM"
echo "kernel banner found $hits times in $uploaded_bytes compressed bytes" >&2
# The step's timeoutSeconds is this value, and SSM kills the whole command when
# it expires. One capture used to have the entire budget; two attempts share it.
# Rather than let a second attempt be killed mid-stream - which yields neither a
# capture nor a diagnostic, only a timed-out command - the loop below refuses to
# start an attempt it cannot finish, using the previous attempt's own duration as
# the estimate. Attempts stream the same amount of RAM, so that estimate is the
[ "$total" -gt 0 ] || fail 'memoryAcquisitionTools is empty - nothing to acquire with'
# No later tool would fit either - they all stream the same RAM - so
# stop here and say so, naming the setting that fixes it.
echo "not starting $tool: ${remaining}s of the ${BUDGET_SECONDS}s step budget remain and the previous attempt needed ${last_attempt_seconds}s. Raise ssmExecutionTimeout." >&2
if ! lime_resolve ; then reasons="$reasons lime:unavailable"; continue; fi
if ! lime_start ; then lime_cleanup; reasons="$reasons lime:did-not-listen"; continue; fi
if ! avml_resolve ; then reasons="$reasons avml:unavailable"; continue; fi
echo "unknown acquisition tool '$tool' - supported values are lime and avml" >&2
# Which tool produced the evidence belongs with the evidence. The object is
# versioned, so a rejected attempt remains as a previous version rather than
# --expected-size only sizes the multipart chunks, it does not validate what
# arrived, so the uploaded object is checked by verify_capture below.
# Every process substitution redirects its own stdout. A substitution
# inherits tee's stdout, which is the pipe feeding sha256sum, and `aws s3 cp`
# writes progress and a final 'upload: - to s3://...' there unconditionally -
# which is how the published digest came to be the hash of the capture
# tr bounds grep's line length. A memory image contains no newline for
# gigabytes and grep buffers a whole line: 1.5 GiB of RSS for 1 GB of input,
# measured with GNU grep 3.8. On a capture the size of the instance's own RAM
# that is an OOM kill, which closes tee's pipe and, with pipefail, fails the
# capture. grep is not given -m1 for the same reason.

if "$streamer" | tee >(gzip | s3cp ".lime.gz" --expected-size "$S3_EXPECTED_SIZE" --metadata "$meta" --acl bucket-owner-full-control --only-show-errors >/dev/null) >(LC_ALL=C tr -c '[:print:]' '\n' | LC_ALL=C grep -c 'Linux version ' > "$banner_probe" 2>/dev/null) | sha256sum | s3cp "_sha256.txt" --acl bucket-owner-full-control --only-show-errors ; then
echo "$tool failed while streaming the capture" >&2

fail "no acquisition tool produced a usable capture after $attempt attempt(s):$reasons. The attempts are preserved as versions of {{s3ArtifactLocation}}/linux_memcapture.lime.gz for inspection. Re-acquire; no symbol table can make an empty capture analysable."
echo "memory captured with $captured on attempt $attempt of $total"
